Throat
throht
noun
From the Saxon throte, the passage of the neck; rendering the Hebrew garon, the gullet or windpipe, and the Greek larugx, the larynx — the channel through which both breath and speech proceed.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The throat is the passage through which speech comes out of a man, and Scripture makes it the most damning exhibit in the case against him. David, describing his enemies, does not begin with their deeds: “there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is very wickedness; their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue” (Psa 5:9). The figure is deliberately foul. An open sepulchre is a grave with the stone rolled away, exhaling the stench of what lies rotting inside; so the throat, opened in speech, releases the corruption of the heart. Paul takes that verse up and sets it in the middle of his indictment of the whole race — Jew and Gentile, all under sin — where throat, tongue, lips, and mouth are arraigned in sequence (Rom 3:13). This is the doctrine of total depravity taken to the organ of speech: not that every man says the worst thing possible, but that the channel itself is defiled at the source, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. The throat has a second and gentler use: it is what fails in prolonged prayer — “I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried” (Psa 69:3), a psalm the Gospels apply to Christ. And it is what a hard man seizes: the forgiven servant took his fellow by the throat over an hundred pence (Mat 18:28), the mercy he had received never reaching his hands.

Webster 1828 Definition

The anterior part of the neck, and the passage through which breath and speech proceed; in Scripture a figure for the corruption of the heart made audible.

expand to see more

THROAT, n. The anterior part of the neck of an animal, in which are the gullet and windpipe, or the passages for the food and breath.

Saxon throte; hence to throttle, to seize or stop the throat.

Hebrew garon, the gullet; Greek larugx, the larynx, the organ of the voice.

An open sepulchre: a figure for speech that exhales the corruption within (Psa 5:9; Rom 3:13).

To take by the throat, to seize violently, as the unmerciful servant did his fellow (Mat 18:28).

Key Scripture

Psa 5:9 — "For there is no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part is very wickedness; their throat is an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue."

Rom 3:13 — "Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:"

Psa 69:3 — "I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God."

Mat 18:28 — "But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest."

Modern Corruption

Rom 3:13 is emptied wherever man is assumed basically good and speech-sin is relocated from the fallen heart to the hearer’s offence, so that words are judged by reception rather than by truth.

expand to see more

Two corruptions meet at this word. The first is the denial of total depravity. Modern religion, evangelical as often as liberal, works from the premise that man is fundamentally decent and occasionally errs, so Rom 3:13 must be softened into a description of unusually bad men rather than an indictment of the race. Paul allows no such escape: he stacks the psalms deliberately — none righteous, none that understandeth, throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet — and concludes that every mouth may be stopped and all the world become guilty before God. The doctrine is not that men are as bad as they could be, but that no faculty came through the fall undefiled, the organ of speech least of all. The second corruption follows from the first: when depravity is denied, sins of speech are no longer measured against God’s law but against the offence taken by the hearer. Words become right or wrong according to who was hurt and how loudly, so that flattery and cowardice pass unrebuked while plain truth is treated as an injury. Scripture judges speech by its source and its truth, not by its reception.

Recover the sepulchre and the remedy together. The image is intended to disgust, because a man will not seek a Saviour for a habit he thinks is a manner of speaking. If the throat is an open grave, the problem is not vocabulary but a corpse, and no course in communication will cure it — only a new heart, out of whose abundance a new mouth speaks. That is exactly the order of Rom 3: the indictment ends at verse 20 so that the righteousness of God without the law may begin at verse 21. Then let the redeemed use the throat as Christ used it. Psa 69:3 shows a dried throat worn out with crying unto God, and that psalm is the Gospels’ own commentary on His passion; He wearied His voice in prayer for those whose voices were raised against Him. And let Mat 18:28 stand as the permanent warning: a man may have been forgiven ten thousand talents and still have hands at his brother’s throat. Forgiveness that never reaches the grip is not forgiveness received.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The passage of breath and speech; Scripture’s figure for the heart’s corruption made audible, and an open grave in the indictment of the race.

expand to see more

Throat — Saxon throte, the passage of the neck; whence throttle.

Hebrew garon, the gullet (Psa 5:9); Greek larugx, the voice-organ (Rom 3:13).

An open sepulchre — a grave unstopped, exhaling what rots within.

Paul quotes Psa 5:9 in the arraignment of the whole race (Rom 3:10–19).

A dried throat marks prolonged prayer (Psa 69:3); a seized throat marks unforgiveness (Mat 18:28).

Usage

"The throat is an open sepulchre — the corruption is in the heart, not merely the vocabulary."

"Rom 3:13 indicts the race, not a class of unusually wicked men."

"Psa 69:3’s dried throat belongs to the Man of sorrows praying for His enemies."
